news.Title: Lam Research (LRCX) Q1 2027 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Wed, Oct. 21, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Vice President of Investor Relations - Ram Ganesh

President and Chief Executive Officer - Tim Archer

Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer - Doug Bettinger

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Please also note, today's event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Ram Ganesh, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Ram Ganesh: Thank you, and good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the Lam Research quarterly earnings conference call. With me today are Tim Archer, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Doug Bettinger, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. During today's call, we will share our overview on the business environment, and we will review our financial results for the September 2026 quarter and our outlook for the December 2026 quarter. The press release detailing our financial results was distributed a little after 1:00 P.M. Pacific Time. The release and the accompanying presentation slides for today's call can be also found on the investor section of the company's website.

Today's presentation and Q&A include forward-looking statements based on our current beliefs, expectations, and assumptions. These statements are subject to risks and uncertainties, and actual results could differ materially from those expressed or implied in such statements. For a discussion of factors that could cause actual results to differ materially, please refer to the risk factors in our most recently filed periodic reports on Form 10-K and Form 10-Q, and subsequent filings with the SEC and the cautionary statement in the accompanying presentation slides. Today's discussion of our financial results will be presented on a non-GAAP financial basis unless otherwise specified. A detailed reconciliation between GAAP and non-GAAP results can be found in the accompanying presentation slides.

This call is scheduled to last until 3:00 P.M. Pacific Time. A replay of this call will be made available later this afternoon on our website. With that, I will hand the call over to Tim.

Tim Archer: Thanks, Ram, and thank you to everyone joining us today. In the September quarter, Lam again delivered record revenue and profitability. Gross margin, operating margin, and EPS all reached new highs, with operating margin topping 40% for the first time. Our performance throughout the year reflects the broad strength of our product portfolio and a relentless focus on operational execution as AI continues to drive unprecedented semiconductor demand and increasing device complexity. Including the midpoint of our December quarter guidance, we expect calendar year 2026 systems revenue to grow well over 40% year-on-year. Rising deposition and etch intensity across all device types and advanced packaging solutions is continuing to drive greater opportunity for Lam.

Story Continues

Over the past few years, increasing device complexity and a push towards greater 3D scaling have driven a four-point expansion of our served available market, or SAM, as a percentage of WFE. When combined with share gains from products addressing this growing SAM, we expect 2026 to mark our third consecutive year of WFE outperformance. For calendar year 2026, we expect WFE in the mid $150 billion range. Our preliminary 2027 WFE outlook is for more than $200 billion of spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND.

As we move into calendar year 2027, we see clean room space availability and supply chain constraints for certain components continuing to limit chip makers and equipment companies' ability to fully meet end demand. We are actively working with our suppliers to accelerate their capacity expansion plans, and are confident Lam is well-positioned to deliver on the strong demand we see ahead. Underpinning our outlook for WFE growth is the continued rapid adoption of AI by enterprises and consumers. It is reported that average weekly token usage is up roughly 250-fold in the past 18 months. As AI moves increasingly towards autonomous agentic workflows, demand for compute, memory, and storage solutions continues to expand.

For example, in NAND, AI performance and economics are driving demand for multiple tiers of storage, each optimized for different workloads. QLC today provides cost-effective storage for rapidly growing AI data volumes. TLC storage is used as a high-bandwidth tier for context memory and KV cache workloads. And SLC class NAND is emerging for low latency, high-speed access in agentic AI. We believe adoption of an SLC storage tier could become a meaningful driver of NAND wafer capacity. Converting from TLC to SLC class devices reduces bits per device by roughly 3 times.

Said differently, for each percentage point mix shift of NAND bits to SLC class devices, approximately 2% more installed wafer capacity will be needed to support the same bit demand. Incremental growth in bit demand would further amplify wafer capacity requirements. We expect all three storage tiers to grow, increasing the value and strategic importance of NAND. We believe Lam is best positioned to benefit from this inflection. We have the industry's largest installed base of NAND systems and a comprehensive product portfolio spanning all critical deposition and etch steps. Any increase in NAND bit demand, whether satisfied through installed base upgrades or capacity additions, will generate additional need for Lam's tools and technology.

Foundry logic and DRAM are seeing a similar device-level evolution to satisfy AI's emerging performance requirements. From advanced patterning and backside power to next-generation packaging, we see billions of dollars of potential SAM expansion and share gain opportunities for Lam in the years ahead. We are seeing the impact of our targeted investments in foundry logic and DRAM products in our calendar year 2026 results. These two market segments have accounted for approximately 80% of Lam's systems revenue growth year-to-date. A good example is our focus on advanced patterning requirements for foundry logic and DRAM.

With each technology node bringing more stringent EUV pattern fidelity and defectivity requirements, Lam's Akara etch, conductor etch and Aether dry resist tools are being paired to deliver unprecedented scaling capability. Importantly, these tools are also helping improve the productivity of DRAM scaling at a time when maximizing fab output is a critical priority for our customers. Multiple chip makers are adopting Akara for its ability to etch very high aspect ratio features with exceptional profile control, while at the same time delivering up to a 50% reduction in wafer-to-wafer and lot-to-lot variability, and up to a 50% gain in wafer output per fab footprint.

Similarly, Lam's Aether dry resist solution has demonstrated sub-10 nanometer resolution at the highest pattern density and fidelity with High-NA EUV. It helps achieve this result while requiring 10% lower exposure dose, improving scanner productivity and reducing patterning cost per wafer. Aether solutions are already ramping in HBM high volume manufacturing with Low-NA EUV, and we see additional insertion opportunities ahead across both DRAM and foundry logic customers. As a result, we now expect cumulative Aether-related revenue to reach approximately $2.5 billion by the end of the decade, roughly $1 billion above our prior expectations. Backside power is another example of where Lam's strength in deposition and etch is evident.

Separating power and signal routing allows for thicker backside metallization to reduce resistance and improve power efficiency. Implementation increases process complexity, driving the need for more deposition, plating, and etch steps. As customers ramp backside power at 2 nanometer and below, our production-proven Vector, Sabre, and Flex tools are well-suited to the task. Vector provides industry-leading footprint density and wafer-to-wafer repeatability with its unique quad architecture. Sabre is the global industry benchmark for electroplating due to its high productivity and superior on-wafer performance. Flex delivers high throughput dielectric etch with low defect levels, leveraging its differentiated small volume chamber design and confined plasma.

New materials such as molybdenum are also being introduced to enable more efficient electrical connections between the backside and front side of the wafer. For this emerging application, our Halo tool is gaining traction by enabling both plasma and thermal processes within a single chamber while delivering industry-leading productivity. We are gaining share in this expanding backside power SAM opportunity and recently secured tool of record wins for all four products at a leading customer. In advanced packaging, our market-leading Syndion product is winning advanced logic in HBM TSV applications. Syndion's differentiated hardware design enables rapid process switching to deliver highly uniform TSV profiles, smooth sidewalls, and high volume productivity. Recently, we attained four new positions across multiple customers.

Our Striker ALD product also achieved multiple TSV liner wins due to the film's superior step coverage and low etch rate. Beyond TSV applications, we secured additional Vector and VECTOR TEOS 3D wins for high-adhesion bonding films and interdie gap fill applications by delivering lower defectivity for thick film deposition. With its high deposition and etch intensity, advanced packaging has become a major growth driver for Lam. For next-generation AI and high-performance computing devices, customers are increasingly turning their sights towards panel-level packaging to scale manufacturing. Our panel-level packaging portfolio continues to gain momentum across fan-out packaging, glass core substrates, and emerging substrate and interposer architectures.

To date, we have shipped panel plating systems to more than 20 customers worldwide across panel sizes ranging from 300 by 300 millimeter-600 by 600 millimeter. Customers continue to select our Kallisto platform for its differentiated coplanarity and plating uniformity performance across bumps, pillars, and redistribution layers. Kallisto is also well-positioned to benefit from increasing adoption of glass core substrates through emerging through-glass via applications. Given our customer engagement, installed base growth, and technology leadership, we expect to achieve panel-level packaging market share that surpasses the strong position we already hold in current wafer-level packaging. Finally, turning to CSBG, we are set to exit calendar year 2026 with solid momentum, with annual revenue expected to grow more than 30% year-over-year.

This is more than twice the rate of our long-term target set at our last Analyst Day. Growth is broad-based across upgrades, spares, and services, supported by high fab utilization and customers' continued focus on installed base efficiency. The value we are delivering with Equipment Intelligence and Dextro Cobots recently helped us secure performance-based service contracts with multiple memory manufacturers. We expect CSBG momentum to continue in calendar year 2027, with revenue growing over 15% year-over-year. To wrap up, we believe the industry is in the early stages of a multi-year investment cycle, with customer visibility extending through 2028. Increasing manufacturing complexity, new materials integration, and advanced packaging are driving higher deposition and etch intensity across device segments.

Our technology leadership, growing installed base, and strategic investments in product innovation and manufacturing capacity position Lam to capitalize on these inflections and drive sustained outperformance. Thank you, and here's Doug.

Doug Bettinger: Great. Thank you, Tim Archer. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining our call today during what I know is a very busy earnings season. We were pleased with our continued strong execution in the September quarter, resulting in our fifth consecutive quarter of record revenue, as well as record gross margin, operating margin, and earnings per share. September quarter revenue was $8.22 billion, which was up 22% sequentially and up 54% from the same period in 2025. The deferred revenue balance at quarter end was $2.66 billion, which was an increase of $227 million from the June quarter. This grew primarily due to increased sales volume, and it was partially offset by a decrease in customer down payments.

From a market segment perspective, September quarter systems revenue in memory was 46%, which was consistent with the prior quarter. On a dollar basis, this represented a record level for memory, and it was up 120% from the same period in 2025. Within memory, non-volatile memory accounted for 26% of our systems revenue, up from the June quarter's level of 23%. On a dollar basis, NAND revenue increased approximately 40% sequentially as the industry continued spending on conversions to 256-layer and above class devices. We are seeing initial spending on 384-layer class devices.

DRAM revenue reached a record, growing sequentially on a dollar basis, but down a little bit on a percentage basis from 23% of systems revenue in the June quarter to 20% in the September quarter. DRAM spending remained focused on technology additions and upgrades across the 1α, 1β, and 1γ nodes that is enabling DDR5, LPDDR5, and more importantly, high-bandwidth memory. Foundry also achieved record revenue. Its share of systems revenue increased to 46% from 44% in the June quarter. Strength in the quarter was driven by investment in leading-edge nodes, including advanced packaging, as well as mature node spending in China.

Finally, Logic and Other were 8% of our systems revenue in the September quarter, slightly down from the prior quarter's level of 10%. Most of the spending here was targeted at leading-edge process nodes. Let me now discuss the regional composition of our total revenue. China contributed 35% of revenue, up from the June quarter level of 26%. We saw strong investments here by both domestic and multinational customers. In the December quarter, we expect China will represent a significantly lower percentage of our total revenue compared with the September quarter. Korea's contribution to revenue in the September quarter remained unchanged from the June quarter level at 20%.

The Taiwan region contributed 18% of revenue, down from the June quarter at 27%. The Customer Support Business Group generated a fourth consecutive quarter of record revenues at nearly $2.5 billion in the September quarter. This was up slightly from the June quarter and 40% higher than the same period in 2025. Each component of CSBG remains strong with the prior quarter. Turning to the gross margin performance. The September quarter came in at an all-time record of 52.4%, improving from the June quarter level of 52% due to favorable customer and product mix. Additionally, we continue to balance our cost and pricing postures.

Operating expenses for the June quarter were $1 billion, up from the prior quarter amount of $916 million. The increase was primarily driven by higher incentive compensation due to our increased profitability levels. We are also investing incremental resources to support growing programs like Akara, Halo, Panel Form Factors, and Dextro. R&D accounted for approximately two-thirds of our total operating expenses. Operating margin for the September quarter was another record at 40.2% compared to the June quarter level of 38.4%. This improvement reflected stronger gross margins and continuing operating leverage as our business scales. The non-GAAP tax rate was 16.5% for the quarter, compared to 11% in the June quarter and in line with our expectations.

The increase was primarily driven by a higher U.S. tax rate on foreign earnings, as well as expected shifts in the geographic mix of income. We expect the tax rate to remain in this range for the December quarter and likely beyond. I'd encourage everyone to make sure they have their earnings models updated to this higher tax rate. Other income and expense for the September quarter was approximately $16 million in income, compared with $19 million in expense in the June quarter. The improvement in OI&E was due to foreign exchange fluctuations, higher interest income, as well as favorability in our venture portfolio.

As we've talked about in the past, you should expect to see some variability in OI&E quarter to quarter dictated by market factors. For the September quarter, diluted earnings per share were a record at $2.20. The diluted share count was roughly 1.26 billion shares, which was relatively unchanged with the June quarter. Let me pivot to capital return. We allocated approximately $1 billion to share repurchases, and we paid $325 million in dividends in the September quarter. During the quarter, we entered into an accelerated share repurchase structure that we'll continue to execute in the December quarter. We returned approximately 41% of free cash flow in the quarter and 59% in the calendar year to date.

I would point out that we also used $750 million to pay down maturing debt during the year. Our long-term plans remain to return 85% of free cash flow to shareholders. We have $3 billion remaining on our board-authorized share repurchase program. Our cash and short-term investments totaled $7.5 billion at the end of the September quarter, which was up from $5.6 billion at the end of the June quarter. The factors behind the increase were cash from operating activities, partly offset by our capital return activities as well as capital expenditure. The September quarter was also a record for our free cash flow, coming in at $3.24 billion in the quarter.

As I mentioned last quarter, we have been increasing our cash levels a little bit to support growing business volumes as well as capital investments in this growing demand environment. Day sales outstanding were 63 days in the September quarter, a decrease from 72 days in the June quarter. Inventory at the September quarter end totaled $4.6 billion, which was an increase of $274 million from the June quarter, as we are building inventory to meet the expected future demand for our products. Nonetheless, inventory turns continued to strengthen to 3.4x versus 3x in the prior quarter. I would just mention this was the highest level of inventory turns in nearly seven years.

Our non-cash expenses for the September quarter included approximately $115 million in equity compensation, $106 million in depreciation, and $16 million for amortization. Capital expenditures in the September quarter were $258 million, which was up from the June quarter at $189 million. Capital spending grew as we continue to increase our lab infrastructure and expand our manufacturing facilities globally. We ended the September quarter with approximately 24,300 regular full-time employees, which was a growth of approximately 1,900 people from the prior quarter. Headcount increased primarily in our factory and field teams to support expanding manufacturing activities and growing tool installations. We also added headcount in R&D. Let us turn to our non-GAAP guidance for the December 2026 quarter.

We are expecting revenue of $8.6 billion ± $400 million. I would mention that this revenue guide would have been a bit higher if not for some near-term supply chain constraints that we are actively managing. We are expecting gross margin of 52.5% ± 1% point. This is improving a little bit in spite of headwinds related to customer mix. We are expecting operating margin of 40.5% ± 1% point. Finally, earnings per share of $2.33 ± $0.15, based on a share count of approximately 1.253 billion shares. Let me wrap up. We continue to execute our strategy for outperformance, delivering another quarter of record revenue and profitability.

Operating margin exceeded 40% for the first time in our history, and we are guiding for this to expand slightly. We are increasing R&D investment to strengthen the already strong product portfolio that we have. We are also investing in the infrastructure needed to support the growing demand we expect in the future. These activities continue to deliver a return on invested capital level that is comfortably above the competition. Operator, that concludes our prepared remarks. Tim and I would now like to open up the call for questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then one on your telephone keypad. If you are using a speakerphone, we ask that you please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If at any time your question has been addressed and you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then two. Once again, we do ask that you please limit yourself to one question and a single follow-up. Today's first question comes from Timothy Arcuri at UBS. Please go ahead.

Timothy Arcuri: Thanks a lot. Doug, I do not think I have ever seen a quarter where you grew systems 35% QoQ, so kudos on that. You did talk about the near-term constraints. I guess you can see that from payables. I think payables were up like $1.3 billion. Can you just give us a sense? Is it fair to say this is costing you $300 million-$400 million? Is that a reasonable number to assume that is costing you in the guidance for December, and do you get that back in March? Do you actually get that back? Thanks.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Tim, that is a good question. I am not going to put a specific number on it. In the script, I said it would have been a little bit higher. So it would have been a little bit higher. And yeah, Tim, to the extent that it is something we would have shipped in December, because of timing, we will ship that in the March quarter.

Timothy Arcuri: Okay, Doug. Can you just talk about there was a call hosted by a big memory company today, and they were talking about 4F².

Doug Bettinger: Yeah.

Timothy Arcuri: They were saying that they're going to prioritize 3D DRAM rather than 4F², and your stock traded down, which was a bit odd to me. It seems that people don't really understand what your position is there. So Tim, I wonder, maybe you can talk about that. Can you talk about how you do for in a 3D world versus a 4F² world and what you're seeing in terms of your customers' DRAM roadmaps. Thanks, Tim.

Tim Archer: Sure. Obviously, we don't know exactly what the reaction was or why people would have reacted in that way because we've said for a long time that as all device architectures go 3D, etch and deposition intensity rises. Now, I would say that in some ways, interestingly, the longer it takes to get there, the more we're seeing momentum for some of our other scaling activities. We focused on this, even in this call, advanced patterning.

If you want to extend the current architecture in which patterns are getting even smaller, that's why we're starting to see this uptick in processes like Aether, processes like Akara for conductor etch, the processes that are needed to etch and create those smaller structures. I would say in the short term, etch and dep intensity are rising, and if really we're making a leap right from 6F² into 3D DRAM, then etch and dep intensity is going to rise even faster, even sooner than we would have thought, and that's a great thing.

Timothy Arcuri: Okay, Tim. Thank you.

Tim Archer: Yep. Thanks, Tim.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from Melissa Weathers at Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.

Melissa Weathers: Hi. Thanks so much for the question. I wanted to also ask on the supply constraints. I think you said you're working with your supply chain to make sure some of those bottlenecks get resolved. Can you just give a little more color on what actions you're taking? Could you consider any co-investments or help on the capital side with those guys? Just what needs to happen to relax those constraints?

Doug Bettinger: Listen, Melissa. We're always working with our supply chain to make sure they're ready for the demand environment that we see. But given how strong things have been, we're seeing a little bit of tightness. I'm not going to get into specifically where it is, except I would tell you that we're managing it, just like we always do. We'll continue to do that, but it just got a little bit tight in the quarter. I have every expectation we'll effectively manage this as well as anybody in the industry will. If we needed to make some level investments, we'd be open to that.

But frankly, a lot of our suppliers are well-capitalized and can manage this on their own from a financial standpoint. I don't know, Tim, would you add anything? No, I think that's correct.

Tim Archer: For those of us who were around during the COVID shortages, this is nothing like that. We learned a lot of lessons during that period. In fact, just in the last two months, we've hosted a couple of big events with our global suppliers to really lay out what we have in terms of expectations for growth into the next couple of years. Where you can run into problems is within our own products, as we talked about etch and deposition intensity increasing in certain parts of our business, like we talked about advanced packaging, for instance, really being a major driver of growth for Lam.

You can find certain suppliers that are seeing percentage growth of our demand to them rising even much faster than Lam itself is growing. I think we have been very clearly communicating that to those suppliers and really asking for transparency to the help they need to keep up with the pace that we're dragging in the industry. I think we'll be caught up very shortly.

Melissa Weathers: Thanks for that. On the NAND spending cycle, and that upgrade opportunity that you guys have been talking about, you pulled it in last quarter. It's nice to hear about the 384-layer devices that I think you guys are shipping to. Can you update us on what inning you think we're at in that NAND upgrade cycle? What trends are you seeing? Maybe any forward-looking comments on the SLC and some of those new opportunities.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, there's still room to go on the upgrade cycle. In fact, when you're in a period of high demand, actually taking tools offline to do the upgrade sometimes is also a scheduling challenge for customers and for us.

Tim Archer: I'd say that we're working our way through that, and we said that we would be finishing that in 2027. But we also pointed out that then you just roll to sort of the next upgrade cycle. Remember, that upgrade was from the 128-layer to kind of into the 200-layer class devices. As you just mentioned, people are already moving into the 300 and 400-layer devices. We've been engaged on those in R&D for quite some time.

But I think the real thing we wanted to point out today is that while we used to just talk about layer counts as the driver for Lam equipment demand and wafer capacity needs, now you're really seeing this separation of storage tiers and each of the devices within NAND starting to be more specialized to different workloads within AI. That actually, just like it did in DRAM with HBM and the impact on bits that could be manufactured per wafer, you're starting to see the performance needs of AI start to create a need for higher performance, low latency devices.

I think we just had a customer talk in some detail about that opportunity, and I think that's going to drive NAND wafer capacity demand, and intensity for Lam's equipment. Thanks, Melissa.

Melissa Weathers: Thank you.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Krish Sankar with TD Cowen. Please go ahead.

Krish Sankar: Yeah, hi. Thanks for taking my question. I have two of them. Doug or Tim, when I look at your Q4 guide, I understand you are talking about mid-$150 billion WFE, but the implied WFE for Q4 is like almost $180 billion or so. I am just wondering, are there any episodic revenues in Q4, or is some of the price increases that the front-end semi equipment companies are doing impacting Q4 and kind of making the WFE number larger? Then I have a quick follow-up.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Krish. No, there is nothing unique or one-off or episodic, to use your word, in the December quarter. It is just consistent with customer demand, frankly. Like I alluded to, it would have been a little bit higher if not for some of these supply chain constraints, but there is not anything one-off.

Krish Sankar: Got it, Doug. Then just a quick follow-up. I think in your prepared comments you mentioned China would be significantly lower in the December versus September. Kind of wondering, can you quantify that? How will the mix look like? Because seems like September quarter was a surprise on the upside with both multinationals and domestics coming in.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Krish. To us, it wasn't a surprise. It was exactly as expected. I mean, the domestic customers in September were strong, but so were the global multinationals. I expect that in December we'll be meaningfully down, driven by the domestic customers in China. I expect in the December quarter, the multinationals in China likely continue to be reasonably strong, but the percent of revenue in China will be meaningfully down in the December quarter.

Krish Sankar: Thanks a lot, Doug.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Krish.

Operator: All right, next question today comes from Harlan Sur at JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Harlan Sur: Yeah, good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. On CSBG, 36% growth first nine months of this year, full year outlook greater than 30%. Very, very strong. The growth tailwinds, I assume higher spares as customer utilizations are at record levels, higher sales of higher dollar value upgrades for NAND, and maybe strength in Reliant, as the mature sectors of the market start to come back. Of course, you have your Equipment Intelligence services offerings. Can you guys just rank order these growth drivers? More importantly, on a year-over-year basis, how much higher are CSBG operating margins? I am just wondering if mix and volume dynamics within CSBG are contributing to the strong overall operating margin profile.

Tim Archer: Yeah. I will let Doug talk about the rank order in terms of financial impact in the short term, but if I were to rank order them in terms of my excitement, clearly as we have talked about, we see Equipment Intelligence, the cobot-driven maintenance, the performance-based service contracts we talked about as really kind of the new part of our CSBG business that is really catching on. We are in an environment right now where just as there was an earlier question about if people are trying to shrink devices even faster to get more bits or more performance out. That creates an intolerance to variability in the process, whether that is in the process control or the maintenance.

That is exactly where Equipment Intelligence and cobots come into play. So we are seeing strong pull for that element, and that is something new for our CSBG business. I am very excited about that becoming a bigger growth driver for us than it has been in the past. I will let Doug talk about upgrades, spares, and everything else.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Harlan, we do not specifically give you hard numbers on each of the individual subcomponents. What I would tell you relative to strength of each of them, though, given how strong utilization in the industry spares and service are just humming along, as you would expect. I have always said spares is the biggest individual component, and that continues to be true. But I am not going to be specific on the other ones. What you alluded to is right. Given where we are at in the NAND conversion/upgrade cycle, that portion of the business continues to be strong. Yes, Reliant did quite nicely last quarter given the strength of investment at mature node spending.

I expect you will see all of these trends continue into next year.

Harlan Sur: Yeah, I appreciate that. As a follow-up, the supply tightness in leading-edge foundry logic is creating tightness in mature and specialty nodes, analog, power, microcontrollers. Foundry supply here is tightening very rapidly, right? It looks like mature foundry suppliers, internal IDM factories, they are all increasing capacity. You just said that this is reflected in your Reliant business, but if I exclude China, are you anticipating this segment of your customer base to grow this year?

Doug Bettinger: Probably not in a meaningful way this year, Harlan. I do expect as we get into next year that mature spending outside of China will be strong because of the dynamics you were just referring to. I am not sure that it is really sticking out quite yet in 2026.

Harlan Sur: Got it. Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Harlan Sur.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from Srini Pajjuri with RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Srini Pajjuri: Thank you. Tim, I am looking at your systems business growth. I think last year you were up 40%, and then this year you are probably going to grow 45%, both well above the WFE growth. Looking out to next year, given your $200 billion plus outlook, roughly 30%, let us say. I suspect you expect to outgrow that market next year as well. Can you talk about what are the drivers? Is it driven by any particular end market like NAND or DRAM or any product line or anything else you can comment on would be helpful.

Tim Archer: Yeah, I guess at a very general level, I would say it is driven by the increase in deposition and etch intensity across all devices. If there were a few things I would point out, just as maybe obvious trends in the market, Lam's exposure in the advanced packaging space is extremely high, and I think advanced packaging continues to play an even more vital role in just about every device that is feeding into AI today. That is, I think, a great position where we will see outperformance. We talked even about that extending into panel level. It really is in every device. You see NAND layers growing. You see new architectures coming to NAND.

We talked a little bit about the emergence of SLC class, and you are starting to hear from our customers. Foundry logic, we have talked about success in gate-all-around. We invested four or five years ago in an entire set of products focused on improving our position in foundry logic and DRAM. I commented on the fact that today, those products are driving a significant portion of our growth here in the years in which foundry logic and DRAM are leading the charge on growth. We are extremely happy with that.

NAND is yet to emerge as to its full potential from our perspective, and I think you are starting to hear about it and the strategic role it can play in AI. I do not know. It is hard to project exactly. We would love to see all the devices grow, but I think the single greatest theme is, regardless of which device we are talking about, deposition and etch will play a greater role in 2027. If you think about We had this model, which was the $100 billion of AI CapEx being about $10 billion in WFE.

The important thing is that $10 billion next year, Lam's opportunity in that $10 billion would be even greater than it is this year because of the device evolution. I think that etch intensity is just a way to think about Lam's opportunity.

Srini Pajjuri: Right. Then maybe on the gross margins. Doug, you are guiding actually slight increase despite, you highlighted some customer mix headwinds. I am suspecting

Doug Bettinger: Yes

Srini Pajjuri: that is related to China. I guess on a normalized basis, as we look out to the next few quarters, once China normalizes, how should we think about gross margins? In the past, you did talk about some pricing actions, and of course, you have the cost and efficiency improvements as well. Just curious as to how we should think about gross margins as we go into next year.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, listen, in the near term, Srini, I think you are going to be plus or minus the level that we are at. We did suggest over the next several years, we see an opportunity to expand gross margin in the mid-50s. You kind of triangulate yourself between these two points. But in the near term, it will bounce around generally where it is. Yeah, the things that contributed to our very strong gross margin as well as our expectation of how we are going to drive improvement into the future are new product introductions, right? We have got some very nice technically differentiated new products like Akara and Aether.

We are excited about where that is all going to trend from a profitability standpoint. We've talked about our close-to-customer strategy relative to how we're manufacturing closer to where the fabs are, that's contributed and still have a little bit of juice left to squeeze there. Then we've also talked about the fact that we're working on pricing. All of those things have contributed to getting us to the all-time record level that we printed in the September quarter and levers we're going to keep trying to pull as we go into the future to get to that mid-50s that we've said we're going to drive towards.

Srini Pajjuri: Thanks, Doug.

Doug Bettinger: Thanks, Srini.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from Vivek Arya with Bank of America Securities. Please go ahead.

Vivek Arya: Thanks for taking my question. For the first one, if I look at last year, you were able to consistently expand your WFE expectations. I think you started the year at mid-$130s. Now it is like mid-$150s. I am curious, what helped you increase WFE expectations last year, and then what are the constraints next year that you think can be resolved to help do better than the 30% or so industry growth? I know you mentioned some constraints in the near term. I am curious if they are the same constraints that limit industry growth for next year, or they are different. It is just what can help you do better than this 30% industry WFE growth?

Doug Bettinger: Vivek, I will start and then I will let Tim add. As we have walked through this year, you are absolutely right. We started mid-$130s, and then we went to a little bit more than $140, and then a little more than $150, and then we just took you to mid-$150s. Basically, what we saw happening across all aspects of our customer base is everybody squeezed a little more out of the clean rooms that they had and/or pulled projects in a little bit quicker than maybe they originally intended. That is generally what happened. Frankly, we did exactly the same thing. With the more than 200 number, we are giving you our initial starting point, more than 200.

We normally do not give you this much specificity this early in the year, and we will give you a sharper pencil on that when we get to the earnings call next quarter.

Vivek Arya: Gotcha. For my follow-up, Doug, you mentioned something about an accelerated repurchase plan.

Doug Bettinger: Yep.

Vivek Arya: I think you can all guess what that is due to, but it would help to hear from you also, and if you could help give some sense of what the magnitude is, how long you plan to continue it. I know you mentioned you have $3 billion left in the buyback, but just how much is the ASR component, how long it continues? Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Vivek, the way these accelerated share repurchase structures work is you enter into them, you get some shares up front, and then they execute over time, depending on where the share price is and volatility and things like that. I am not going to disclose actually the start or end date because there are ranges around it. I do not like people to know what we do and how we do it, except I will reinforce for you, it is going to continue to execute in December, and then we will likely be doing other things in the market relative to the buyback, right?

Our medium long-term goals remain unchanged, which is to return 85% of free cash flow to shareholders.

Vivek Arya: Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yep, thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from Atif Malik with Citi. Please go ahead.

Atif Malik: Hi, thank you for taking my questions. The first one for Tim. Tim, I thought your panel-level packaging comments are extremely bullish. You are talking about a share that will exceed the wafer level packaging. Can you just kind of double-click in terms of the industry ramp on panel-level packaging and your products. Are the products the same as wafer level, like Sabre, that will drive this growth?

Tim Archer: Yeah, at a fundamental level, they are similar. I think part of our optimism in this space is, one, it makes sense. Obviously we talked, I think, on the last earnings call about how packages themselves are getting larger, which in many cases they are too big for wafer level packaging, and so panels make sense as you try to assemble bigger and bigger system-level solutions. So we saw that quite a while ago, and we have been investing in panel for several years. I would say we are still, though, in the very early stages. Wafer level packaging is the predominant method.

But as we talked about the shipments to more than 20 customers, you can think of those as really planting the seeds for an industry that I think is going to ultimately assume a fair bit of the packaging work for the industry. The processes that we talked about, we do not call it Sabre in this case, but there is a plating aspect to this and some other processes that I think will do extremely well within panel level.

Atif Malik: Great. Doug, on that +$200 billion wafer fab equipment outlook for next year, your rank order is DRAM, foundry logic, and NAND, which is the same as 90 days ago, but has the gap between DRAM and foundry logic expectations narrowed given some of the announcements on the new logic fabs from foundry and Terafab like?

Doug Bettinger: No, Atif, they really haven't. As you might expect, all of these projects, perhaps, that people are now publicly hearing about, we knew about in advance of that. It really hasn't changed much.

Atif Malik: Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Atif.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question today comes from James Schneider at Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

James Schneider: Good evening. Thanks for taking my question. I was wondering, as you look into 2027, can you maybe frame for us some of the moving pieces that could adjust the WFE outlook higher or lower? How much of it really is your customers' individual spending plans for the different technology or product areas, versus just the general availability of clean room space overall?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, Jim, I'll start, and then I'll let Tim add. When we look in the next year, we see 10 new tier I fabs coming online between the beginning of the year and the end of the year, and they will layer in over time. That's obviously a contributor. This year has been primarily clean room constrained. In that, again, you see, like we said, some emerging supply chain constraints that we're confident we're going to be able to work through effectively, but the whole industry is going to have to work through very similar things. All this, at the end of the day, has to get balanced. Every equipment company needs to be able to supply things.

Clean rooms need to come on schedule. People need to hire and train to make sure they're all ready. The industry's good at doing this, and we're great at doing it. But all of those things have to come into play when you're thinking about what the next year is going to look like.

Tim Archer: Yeah, I think in my prepared remarks, I talked about the fact that we have visibility through 2028. That's really from the demand side. I think that where we're saying it might just be a little bit early to give such a precise number on WFE is simply because we think by the January call, which is the normal time we would give that level of detail, we'll have a better view of clean room schedules, of supply chain constraints, and really be able to hone in on that. But those are the things we're looking at.

Just as this year, we were able to work through those, and I think as we get closer, we'll get a better sense for how the industry is responding.

James Schneider: Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Thanks, Jim.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Stacy Rasgon with Bernstein Research. Please go ahead.

Stacy Rasgon: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my questions. For the first one, I understand that this more than $200 billion WFE next year is a constrained number. Do you guys have a point of view on what that number would be if it was not constrained, if clean rooms were available, if supply chain was not as tight as it is? I guess what I am asking is, what do you think the demand for WFEs in 2027 versus the supply number that you have given?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Listen, Stacy, you always ask these interesting questions. You know what I am going to ask. I love the question nonetheless. Listen, things are going to continue to be constrained, we think, in the next year by the things that we have described. I am not going to put a number on what the unconstrained demand would be. It would be higher. I am not going to give you a precise number. Like I said, we will fine tune what we think the number is and give you a little more specificity on the next quarter call also.

Stacy Rasgon: Okay, that is helpful. For my follow-up, any thoughts on the NAND upgrades relative to the services? It sounded like upgrades were strong. I do not know if that meant that they grew sequence or not. I assume they did because the NAND revenues grew a bunch, but the CSBG revenues were kind of flattish. I thought the upgrades were in CSBG. If that is the case, I guess what I am asking is, did upgrades drive the NAND growth? If they did, what else was going on in CSBG to absorb the growth such that the overall was flat?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Listen, Stacy, upgrades are a part of NAND and also CSBG. NAND also, when you go through these conversions, you need to buy new equipment also. Obviously, there was a contribution in demand spending from new equipment also.

Stacy Rasgon: Was it bigger than the upgrade piece? Sounds like it was.

Doug Bettinger: Both were meaningful contributors.

Stacy Rasgon: Okay. Thank you, guys.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Stacy.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Blayne Curtis at Jefferies. Please go ahead.

Blayne Curtis: Hey, guys. Thanks for squeezing me in. I actually want to ask on the NAND side, you mentioned SLC, that could be a big transition. Is that something you are seeing from customers, or is that still a potential transition?

Tim Archer: I think it is something that you are starting to hear from customers, talked about. Fundamentally, this idea of customizing memory and storage hierarchy to the different workloads, I think is now pretty well understood. I think that this is emerging as one of the potential solutions for low latency NAND access. I think if you go look just in the last recent days and weeks, there has been discussion of SLC+ NAND emerging as part of that stack. For a little bit longer time, there has been discussion also things like high bandwidth flash and the role it can play.

We are really starting to see NAND move from sort of a singular application we have always thought of, to now one in which perhaps the device performances themselves will need to be customized. That will have implications for us, but it will also from a process perspective. But really what we were highlighting here was the impact it would have on wafer capacity needs and therefore perhaps an uptick in NAND equipment demand.

Blayne Curtis: Thanks. I want to ask on advanced packaging, I think you said last time it would grow over 70% for the calendar year, I was curious what the update is. When you look at, it is probably at the smaller end, so you did not mention it, but in terms of that $200 billion outlook, any thoughts on advanced packaging growth next year?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Blayne, 70% for this year is still the right number. I would be stunned if advanced packaging didn't grow nicely next year.

Blayne Curtis: Yeah. Thanks, guys.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Blayne.

Operator: Our next question comes from Shane Brett at Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Shane Brett: Great. Thank you for letting me ask a question. My first question is on Foundry Logic. At your 2025 Analyst Day, you talked about your Foundry Logic SAM per wafer increasing 2x. Just how far are we towards that 2x with the shift from 3 nanometer, 2 nanometer, or if I rephrase that, how high did our SAM grow from 3 nanometer-2 nanometer? Do you think your share gains would accelerate with the transition to 1.4? Thank you.

Tim Archer: Yeah, that 2x was a multi-generational shift. It's a little bit hard to put exactly where we are in that. Maybe halfway through, if I thought about that roadmap that we gave there. But really, as we've moved forward though, we've seen just new emerging applications. I talked about a couple of them today. Clearly, advanced patterning itself is becoming ever more critical. We talked about the growth in Aether. We talked about the use of Akara for conductor etch. Backside power really starting to get a lot more attention, being a very etch and deposition intensive application. We just see a number of elements of that improvement. Then, I commented about how excited I was about advanced packaging.

Advanced packaging is playing a huge role within Foundry Logic and our exposure to the WFE there. I'm just saying Foundry Logic is turning into a good story. The thing we've highlighted over the last couple of calls, though, just to remind you, is the role we play in gate-all-around, our- Strength in ALD, in our strength in surface treatment. Those are areas where I think even at the Analyst Day, we might not have realized just how strong the uptake would be for things like the Argos surface treatment tool.

So I feel like the story just kind of keeps getting better and better the more complex the devices get across all three device types, foundry logic, DRAM, and NAND.

Shane Brett: Got it. For my follow-up, it will be on advanced packaging. SEMICON West, one of your colleagues had a great presentation on breaking the integration wall and advanced packaging for the AI era, with one of the highlights being key challenges to hybrid bonding adoption at scale. Just how does Lam enable hybrid bonding? Is more hybrid bonding better or worse for our advanced packaging share? Thank you.

Tim Archer: Well, I think that we participate in the elements of the process that help enable hybrid bonding. Obviously as a deposition and etch company, we do not do the bonding ourself, but we talked about a number of films, whether it is in the dielectric space or in the metal space, that ultimately play an important role in achieving successful hybrid bonding. There is an opportunity for Lam, through that transition. I think that overall, look the reality is success in advanced packaging, whatever version it is, will lead to greater adoption of advanced packaging, and ultimately, given our very high share position, that is a good thing for us.

Hybrid bonding or no, it is a very etch and deposition intensive process compared to other parts of the semiconductor manufacturing process itself. Thanks, Shane.

Shane Brett: Got it. Thank you very much.

Operator: Our next question today comes from Vijay Rakesh with Mizuho. Please go ahead.

Doug Bettinger: Vijay, are you there?

Operator: Vijay, your line is open, or are you perhaps on mute?

Vijay Rakesh: Oh, I was on mute. Sorry about that. Tim and Doug gave some interesting comments on the NAND side. You mentioned every 1% move to SLC requires about 2% increase in wafer capacity. As we look at next year with the move to SLC and potentially some HBF, any thoughts on how you think what percent of the market moves to SLC? Is it like 5% or how would you see that?

Tim Archer: I think it is too early for us to make any comment on that, and it would be probably something our customers should actually be commenting on. What you can rest assured is that in that sense, the intensity of Lam equipment in manufacturing those devices and those wafers would go up.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. Then a quick follow-up. The advanced packaging side, you mentioned obviously there's a whole CoWoS and EMIB-T coming. I guess Lam has huge opportunities on the metallization pre-clean, TSV, et cetera. Just wondering if there's a way to size that opportunity, as you have done before for every 100,000 wafers of EMIB-T or CoWoS. How would you size that opportunity for Lam? Thanks.

Tim Archer: Yeah, I think maybe we'll take that as an action for some work to still be done. Maybe we're sizing that. We're not prepared to do that today.

Vijay Rakesh: Got it. Thank you. Thanks.

Doug Bettinger: Yep, you bet. Operator, we're going to take one more question.

Operator: Absolutely. Our final question today comes from Brian Chin at Stifel. Please go ahead.

Brian Chin: Hi there. Good afternoon. Thanks for letting us ask a few quick questions here. Maybe Doug, firstly, days of inventory kind of running a little bit over maybe a quarter at the moment. Clearly has drawn down. You said the turns have been really strong. Ideally, where would you want that to be?

Doug Bettinger: Yeah, listen, we are super comfortable where it is right now. As the company scales up, you do get some level of efficiency offsetting that, though, right now we are trying to build inventory in anticipation of the growing demand we see into the next year. But I think we collectively feel pretty good about where we are at 3.4x.

Brian Chin: Okay, great. Maybe just the last question here. Is the $1 billion increase in your Aether revenue outlook reflective more of adding foundry logic and DRAM customers in terms of the adoption of that platform? Or is it more towards existing customers pulling forward introduction of the timing of Aether?

Doug Bettinger: I think it's a little bit of both. There have been some additional customer adoptions, but really it is as you really become POR for something like we mentioned, HBM manufacturing, and the volumes are growing there, the number of tools, and therefore the business just continues to expand. So we feel like we're positioned in production for some of the fast-growing parts of the market, and that's why we're able to take the number up.

Brian Chin: Great. Thank you.

Doug Bettinger: Yeah. Thanks, Brian. Listen, thanks everybody for joining the call today. We're really excited about where the business is performing. We're really excited about what things look like into the next year, and I think we're probably the most excited about a third consecutive year of outperformance and an expectation that we're going to continue to drive those things into the next calendar year. So I know we'll see a lot of you guys in NDRs and conferences in the coming quarter, and we look forward to seeing you. Thanks for joining the call.

Operator: Thank you. That concludes today's conference call. We thank you all for attending today's presentation. You may now disconnect your lines, and have a wonderful day.

news.Title: Meta (META) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Director of Investor Relations - Rob Bevegni

Chief Executive Officer - Mark Elliot Zuckerberg

Chief Financial Officer - Susan J. Li

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Good afternoon. My name is Krista, and I will be your conference operator. Today. At this time, I would like to welcome everyone to Meta's Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All lines have been placed on mute to prevent any background noise. After the speakers' remarks, there will be a question-and-answer session. We ask that you limit yourself to 1 question. And this call will be recorded. Thank you very much. Rob, Bevagni, Meta's Director of Investor Relations, you may begin.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: Thank you. Good afternoon, and welcome to Meta Platform's third quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today to discuss our results are Mark Elliot Zuckerberg, CEO and Susan J. Li, CFO. Our remarks today will include forward-looking statements, which are based on assumptions as of today. Actual results may differ materially as a result of various factors, including those set forth in today's earnings press release and in our quarterly report on Form 10 Q filed with the SEC. We undertake no obligation to update any forward-looking statement. During this call, we will present both GAAP and certain non GAAP financial measures. A reconciliation of GAAP to non GAAP measures is included in today's earnings press release.

Earnings press release and an accompanying investor presentation are available on our website at investor.@.com. And now, I would like to turn the call over to Mark. Alright. Hey, everyone. Thanks for joining today. This has been a busy and exciting few months. Our Family of Apps is now used by 3.64 billion people each day, and we are seeing all time highs in engagement on both Facebook and Instagram driven by strong growth in video. Threads has now overtaken x in monthly actives and to grow quickly. WhatsApp is hitting all time highs and is becoming an increasingly important platform for agents as well.

In the last few months, we have had several major milestones towards our goal of delivering personal superintelligence to everyone. We had 1 of our most successful launches ever with the Muse personal agent, We shipped Muse Wonder as our first frontier model. We shipped several new glasses and gadgets with Muse integration including coming soon to our new audio glasses.

We have been discussing our vision for personal superintelligence for more than a year, I want to help every person have an extremely capable personal agent that understands your goals and can help you achieve them and improve your life in whatever ways you want whether that is improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of. Muse is the product form of this vision. So now we have the foundational technology in place to deliver this. There is still a lot of work ahead, but our initial position is very strong.

Story Continues

In just a month and a half, more than 10 million people in the US and Canada have set up Muse personal agents, Growth continues to be strong, and we have been number 1 in the App Store almost every day. Engagement and retention are also off to a strong start, About 25% of people who have set up Muse use it on any given day. For our earliest adopters, the longer that they use Muse, the better the retention seems to get. So to put this in perspective, this is more than 2x the level that Threads started at or where we believe that other AI apps started at as well.

The most common use case for Muse is shopping. With more than 25% of people who are using Muse engaging in this with an average purchase size of over $200. Plaid told us that they had not seen activity like they are seeing with their connector on any other service before. And in the first week, we had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected. Beyond shopping, the most common connectors are for personal productivity and connecting Muse to your other services like email and calendar.

Now this shows the importance of the Muse secure VM that we have built to provide state-of-the-art privacy and security we are looking forward to following up soon with the Muse confidential VM which will make it so that even Meta cannot see your content. We have also seen that Muse wonder improves quality engagement and retention further, which suggests that as we continue to improve intelligence, Muse will perform better and better over time. Now that Muse has clear product market fit, we are entering a new phase and a more operational phase that is focused on scaling it. The goals for this next phase play to many of Meta's strengths.

We need to do 3 things, scale the product, grow revenue, and optimize compute costs. We expect to grow Muse to serve billions of people. This is both our mission and our strategy. it is our mission in that we believe in putting the power of personal superintelligence in everyone's hands. We believe that is the path to ensuring a positive future for everyone with individual empowerment as the source of prosperity, and balance of power is the foundation for safety. On a values level, we believe that delivering this capability widely is the best thing that we can be doing.

This is also our strategy because we think that billions of muses in a network at scale will be able to get more done for people and businesses by working together. So we would like to create a large scale Muse network as quickly as possible. From a business perspective, the average revenue per American user for our existing Muse users is. Sorry. For our existing Family of Apps users is several hundreds of dollars annually, and we expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place. This will take some time, but we are starting to work on this now.

Our business model will have a few components. For most people, the product should be free, and we will build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate. We expect this will be paid for by businesses. For people who want the most advanced models or to use extra tokens, they subscribe directly and pay. For business owners who want additional features, to use Muse to grow their businesses or for companies that want people to use Muse for work, they will be able to subscribe directly and pay as well.

And for those who want Muse to help improve the personalization and quality of their content and ads across Meta, they will be able to connect to those experiences as well. Just to clarify, the average revenue that I was talking about before is the Family of Apps revenue for our existing Muse users. On the compute side, we are building out the capacity to serve more than a billion people over the next few years. In the near term, Muse is very compute intensive to run. The second theme I would say is that, you know, we are excited about some of the new research bets that we have as we move into sort of a more LLM-oriented AI infrastructure to help us more deeply reason about people's preferences, what they are interested in both across organic content and recommendations, and we expect that we will be able to unlock we will be able to unlock benefits to our ranking and recommendations and from that research too.

So I would say we feel like there is, you know, meaningful runway across all 3 of those things. Your second question was about revenue growth next year.

Mark Elliot Zuckerberg: Yeah. I mean, I can talk briefly about the first 1. I mean, look, It was more than a year ago that I think I wrote the letter about personal superintelligence as the North Star for the work that we are doing here. That we would be able to build the best experience by owning and building and designing ourselves the end to end technology So that includes the models and then the agents. I mean, the vision around the glasses has also been this. I mean, the we have wanted to build the next generation of hardware platforms that we can deliver the best end to end experiences to people. And think that is starting to come together as well, and I think will even more over the coming years. So, I mean, these are long term bets. I feel like this is what we are here to do is make long term technology bets and design the best experiences end to end that we can for billions of people around the world.

And I think as long as we continue to do that, then know, over time, the business takes care of itself as long as, you know, we continue executing well, which I am really proud of the team for how we are how we are doing on that. Thanks, Mark.

Susan J. Li: Your second question was around Muse for small business. And if you click along with dozens of third party connectors that businesses already run on, like Shopify, QuickBooks, Canva, etcetera.

It already understands what businesses sell, brand voice, what customers are asking for, and muse can take actions including analyze ad and content performance, draft campaigns, responses, flag issues, you know, and we are actively listening to our SMB users to understand what their top use cases are. You know, we are seeing them use it for ads optimization, for direct message organizing, use it to expand their sales footprint, to keep their web current based on, you know, things like inventory and new products, to deal with employee load balancing.

So we are we are pretty closely following how business use Muse to make sure that we are being thoughtful about new features that we release in Muse to make it maximally useful and productive for SMBs. I would also say, you know, we have unique touch points to again, you know, I mentioned in my opening remarks, 500 million self identified small businesses. And, you know, we think that many of the investments that we make in consumer products are gonna carry over to help power those businesses also. We have, multiple excellent channels to surface those opportunities to small businesses globally.

So, you know, this is a place where we feel like we have an existing extremely strong platform, and we are very excited about it. And we also, you know, believe the transition to AI has broadly unlocked has broadly unlocked enterprises and new opportunity for us as well.

news.Title: Lam Research Q1 Earnings Call Highlights
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in Lam Research Corporation? Here are five stocks we like better.

Record September-quarter results: Lam Research reported $8.22 billion in revenue, up 22% sequentially and 54% year over year, with record 52.4% gross margin, 40.2% operating margin and $2.20 in non-GAAP EPS.

Strong AI- and memory-driven outlook: Lam forecast December-quarter revenue of $8.6 billion and expects 2027 wafer-fabrication equipment spending to exceed $200 billion, led by DRAM, leading-edge foundry logic and NAND demand.

Growth remains constrained by capacity and supply: Near-term component shortages and clean-room limitations could delay shipments, while China revenue is expected to decline significantly in the December quarter. Lam generated record $3.24 billion in free cash flow and returned approximately 41% of it through buybacks and dividends.

From High Dividend Growth to High Yield, These 3 Stocks Just Boosted Dividend Payouts

Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX) reported record revenue, profitability and earnings per share for its September 2026 quarter, as demand tied to artificial intelligence, advanced semiconductor manufacturing and packaging continued to support spending on deposition and etch equipment.

Revenue for the September quarter totaled $8.22 billion, up 22% sequentially and 54% from the same period in 2025, Chief Financial Officer Doug Bettinger said. The company recorded a gross margin of 52.4%, an operating margin of 40.2% and diluted non-GAAP earnings per share of $2.20, all records. Operating margin exceeded 40% for the first time, according to the company.

→ The AI Sell-Off Continues—These 3 Stocks Keep Raising Guidance Anyway

Analysts Just Raised Price Targets On These 3 Semiconductor Equipment Stocks

"In the September quarter, Lam again delivered record revenue and profitability," President and Chief Executive Officer Tim Archer said. He said AI-driven semiconductor demand and rising device complexity were increasing the intensity of deposition and etch processes across memory, logic and advanced-packaging applications.

December Outlook and WFE Forecast

For the December 2026 quarter, Lam forecast revenue of $8.6 billion, plus or minus $400 million. The company expects gross margin of 52.5%, plus or minus one percentage point; operating margin of 40.5%, plus or minus one percentage point; and earnings per share of $2.33, plus or minus $0.15.

→ Tesla's Roadster Reveal Hints at 2 Much Bigger Moves

Why Lam Research Still Looks Like a Buy After a 300% Rally

Bettinger said the December revenue outlook would have been "a little bit higher" without near-term supply-chain constraints. He did not quantify the impact, but said shipments delayed from the December period because of timing would move into the March quarter.

Story Continues

Lam expects calendar-year 2026 wafer-fabrication equipment, or WFE, spending to be in the mid-$150 billion range. Its preliminary forecast for 2027 calls for more than $200 billion in WFE spending, with percentage growth led by DRAM, followed by leading-edge foundry logic and NAND.

→ Luxury's Middle Market Is Cracking—These 3 Stocks Could Win

Archer said clean-room availability and supply constraints for certain components may limit the industry's ability to fully meet demand in 2027. The company is working with suppliers to expand capacity, he said, and expects to improve the supply situation shortly. Bettinger added that Lam expects 10 new Tier 1 fabs to come online during 2027.

At the midpoint of its December-quarter outlook, Lam expects calendar-year 2026 systems revenue to grow more than 40% year over year. Archer said the company expects 2026 to be its third consecutive year of WFE outperformance, supported by growth in Lam's served available market and product share gains.

Memory and Foundry Demand Drive Growth

Memory represented 46% of September-quarter systems revenue, unchanged from the prior quarter, while foundry accounted for 46%, up from 44%. Logic and other applications represented 8% of systems revenue.

Memory systems revenue reached a record dollar level and increased 120% from a year earlier. NAND accounted for 26% of systems revenue, compared with 23% in the June quarter, as customers continued converting to 256-layer and higher-class devices. NAND revenue rose about 40% sequentially, and Lam said it is seeing initial spending on 384-layer-class devices.

DRAM revenue also reached a record, with spending focused on technology additions and upgrades at the 1α, 1β and 1γ nodes for DDR5, LPDDR5 and high-bandwidth memory. Archer said Lam expects etch and deposition intensity to increase as DRAM architectures become more three-dimensional.

The company also discussed potential new NAND demand related to AI storage tiers. Archer said QLC NAND supports cost-effective data storage, TLC is used for higher-bandwidth context-memory and key-value-cache workloads, and SLC-class NAND is emerging for low-latency access in agentic AI applications.

Lam said shifting NAND production from TLC to SLC-class devices reduces bits per device by roughly three times. For every one-percentage-point shift of NAND bits toward SLC-class devices, about 2% more installed wafer capacity would be needed to support the same bit demand, according to the company.

Technology Investments and Advanced Packaging

Archer said foundry logic and DRAM accounted for about 80% of Lam's systems-revenue growth year to date. The company highlighted demand for its Akara etch, conductor etch and Aether dry-resist products in advanced patterning applications.

Lam said its Aether dry-resist solution has demonstrated sub-10-nanometer resolution with High-NA EUV and can reduce exposure dose by 10%. Aether products are ramping in high-volume HBM manufacturing using Low-NA EUV, Archer said. Lam now expects cumulative Aether-related revenue to reach about $2.5 billion by the end of the decade, approximately $1 billion above its previous expectation.

The company also cited opportunities in backside power delivery, where it has secured tool-of-record wins for four products at a leading customer. In advanced packaging, Lam said its Syndion etch product won four new positions across multiple customers for advanced logic and HBM through-silicon-via applications.

Lam expects advanced-packaging revenue to grow about 70% during calendar 2026. Archer said panel-level packaging is an emerging growth opportunity, with Lam having shipped panel plating systems to more than 20 customers globally. The company expects to achieve panel-level packaging market share exceeding its position in current wafer-level packaging.

Regional Mix, Services and Capital Returns

China represented 35% of September-quarter revenue, up from 26% in the June quarter, due to investments from domestic and multinational customers. Bettinger said China's contribution is expected to be significantly lower in the December quarter, primarily due to lower domestic-customer revenue, while multinational demand in the region should remain reasonably strong.

Korea accounted for 20% of revenue and Taiwan contributed 18%. Lam's Customer Support Business Group generated nearly $2.5 billion in revenue, its fourth consecutive quarterly record and a 40% increase from a year earlier. The company expects full-year 2026 CSBG revenue growth of more than 30%, followed by growth of more than 15% in 2027.

Lam generated record free cash flow of $3.24 billion in the September quarter. It repurchased about $1 billion of shares and paid $325 million in dividends, returning roughly 41% of quarterly free cash flow to shareholders. The company ended the quarter with $7.5 billion in cash and short-term investments and $3 billion remaining under its authorized share-repurchase program.

About Lam Research (NASDAQ:LRCX)

Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ:LRCX) is a semiconductor equipment company that develops and manufactures systems used to fabricate integrated circuits. Its technologies support key stages of wafer processing, helping semiconductor manufacturers create the increasingly complex structures found in memory, logic and other types of chips.

The company's product portfolio includes etch systems, which selectively remove materials from wafers; deposition systems, which apply thin films; and cleaning solutions used to remove contaminants and residue during manufacturing.

news.Title: Cathie Wood Trimmed Ark's Alphabet Stake Even as Google Search Revenue Grew, While Ark Piled Into Rocket Lab Even After Its Neutron Launch Delay. Is Ark Betting Against the Wrong AI Winner?
news.Content:
On Sept. 22, Cathie Wood's Ark Invest bought roughly $25.1 million of Rocket Lab (NASDAQ: RKLB) shares, while selling $5.8 million of Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) stock. However, Rocket Lab has since encountered another setback in its growth plans. On Oct. 14 , the company announced that its Neutron rocket's first launch had been delayed until 2027. Despite this setback, Ark Invest purchased another $9.3 million of Rocket Lab shares on Oct. 15.

Ark's investment decisions highlight the trade-off between Alphabet's established profitability and Rocket Lab's potentially higher, but less certain, long-term growth.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Alphabet's AI investments are showing results

Alphabet's search advertising revenue growth was not driven solely by higher ad prices. The company's paid clicks rose 13% year over year, while average cost per click increased 3% year over year in the second quarter. Google Cloud revenue also jumped 82% year over year to $24.8 billion, and operating income more than tripled to $8.8 billion in the second quarter. These numbers show stronger advertising monetization and profitable cloud growth, although Alphabet doesn't separately disclose AI profits.

Alphabet's upcoming third-quarter results on Oct. 28 could provide further clarity on its AI investments. J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth expects Google Cloud revenue to double year over year, partly driven by solid demand for Google's custom AI chips. However, Alphabet has also guided for $195 billion to $205 billion in capital expenditures for 2026. With such massive spending, sustaining revenue growth while protecting profit margins will be increasingly important.

Why Ark remains interested in Rocket Lab

Ark's investment thesis relies on a possible shortage of launch capacity in the U.S. in the coming years. The investment firm expects Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), better known as SpaceX, could retire its existing Falcon 9 rocket launch system by the end of 2030, while increasingly using its next-generation Starship rocket to support orbital AI data centers. This could create opportunities for competing launch providers, including Rocket Lab, as government agencies, communications providers, and other commercial customers seek alternatives to SpaceX.

Story Continues

Rocket Lab already has evidence of commercial demand. The company has entered a multiyear launch deal with Synspective for 20 launch missions using its operational Electron rockets. The company also exited the second quarter (ending June 30, 2026) with a backlog of $2.36 billion. Rocket Lab's space systems segment, which manufactures satellites, spacecraft components, and related equipment, accounted for nearly 81% of the second-quarter revenue. Hence, Rocket Lab's existing business is not entirely dependent on Neutron's success.

However, realizing Ark's expected launch-market opportunity depends on Neutron becoming commercially successful. Rocket Lab has secured a launch contract with Kepler Communications for satellites supporting on-orbit computing, but the mission is scheduled no earlier than 2028. Hence, even a successful first Neutron launch in 2027 cannot guarantee regular, profitable operations.

Rocket Lab has also raised $1.94 billion by issuing 29.3 million shares to help fund its planned acquisition of Iridium Communications . While the deal could add recurring revenue, the share issuance also dilutes existing shareholders.

Rocket Lab is currently trading at over 39 times trailing-12-month sales, leaving very little room for execution missteps. Alphabet is trading at just close to 9.3 times sales, despite established profitability and more visible AI monetization. Hence, Alphabet currently appears to offer the stronger risk-adjusted AI investment opportunity, although Rocket Lab could deliver greater returns if its ambitious expansion succeeds.
